title: Shelter dogs as reservoirs of international clones of Escherichia coli carrying mcr-1.1 and bla(CTX-M) resistance genes in Lima, Peru
authors: Ayzanoa B, Salvatierra G, Cuicapuza D, Furlan JPR, Sellera FP, Chavez L, Esposito F, Tsukayama P, Lincopan N
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical public health threat worldwide, particularly at the human-animal interface where cross-transmission of critical priority Enterobacterales, such as Escherichia coli, have become increasingly reported. Worryingly, E. coli encoding extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) has been documented in companion animals worldwide. Conversely, the presence of mcr genes, which confer resistance to polymyxins, in bacteria from pets remains more infrequent. In this study, we sequenced and reported on the first genomic data of E. coli strains carrying mcr-1 and/or blaCTX-M genes isolated from rectal swabs of stray dogs in a shelter in the city of Lima, Peru. Antimicrobial susceptibility revealed that E. coli strains exhibited a multidrug resistance profile. In addition to mcr-1 and blaCTX-M genes, other clinically relevant resistance determinants were identified, with notably presence of blaTEM-176 and the novel blaSCO-2 variant. The association of mcr-1.1 and IncI2 plasmid was confirmed. Several virulence genes were detected, classifying strains as putative extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli. Multilocus sequence typing prediction recognized diverse sequence types (ST), including ST155, ST189, ST657, ST746, ST1140, ST3014, and ST7188. This study represents the first report of mcr-positive E. coli in dogs from Peru, emphasizing the need for continuous surveillance and genomic characterization to better understand the transmission dynamics of these critical resistance genes at the human-animal interface. Furthermore, our results provide evidence that stray, and shelter dogs could be a reservoir for the spread of WHO priority pathogens, and/or polymyxin and β-lactam resistance genes, which is a public health and One Health concern that requires appropriate management strategies.

mcqs.q: A Lima shelter screens stray dogs for antimicrobial resistance. Which resistance gene class, detected in this study, confers resistance to polymyxins (last-resort antibiotics) and was newly reported in Peruvian dogs?
o: blaCTX-M (extended-spectrum β-lactamase)
mcr-1 (mobilized colistin resistance)
blaTEM (penicillinase)
blaNDM (New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase)
mcqs.e: The study identified mcr-1 genes conferring polymyxin (colistin) resistance, representing the first report of mcr-positive E. coli in dogs from Peru. blaCTX-M was also found but confers β-lactam, not polymyxin, resistance.

mcqs.q: This study characterizes E. coli from shelter dogs as putative extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC). Which virulence-related finding best supports this classification?
o: Presence of fluoroquinolone resistance genes
Detection of multiple virulence genes alongside international high-risk sequence types
Recovery from gastrointestinal tract exclusively
Absence of plasmid-mediated resistance determinants
mcqs.e: ExPEC classification was supported by detection of multiple virulence genes and diverse high-risk multilocus sequence types (including ST155 and ST189), which are internationally disseminated clones associated with extraintestinal infections.

mcqs.q: In the context of One Health, the most significant public health concern raised by this shelter dog study is:
o: The potential for shelter dogs to transmit parvovirus to humans
The risk that shelter staff could acquire GI infections from E. coli
Shelter dogs serving as reservoirs and potential sources of MDR E. coli with co-resistance to polymyxins and β-lactams for humans
High prevalence of diarrhea in shelter dogs leading to kennel contamination
mcqs.e: The study's key One Health concern is that shelter dogs carrying E. coli with mcr-1 (polymyxin resistance) and blaCTX-M (β-lactam resistance) could transmit these WHO priority pathogens across the human-animal interface, compromising last-resort antibiotics.

title: Streptococcus zooepidemicus in dogs: Exploring a canine pathogen through multilocus sequence typing
authors: Mangano ER, Jones GMC, Suarez-Bonnet A, Waller AS, Priestnall SL
abstract: Streptococcus equi. subsp. zooepidemicus (S. zooepidemicus) associated diseases in dogs have emerged as a significant concern over recent decades. S. zooepidemicus occurs sporadically in dog populations globally, with increased prevalence in shelters/kennels. This study used multilocus sequence typing (MLST) of 149 independent canine S. zooepidemicus isolates to assess associations between sequence type and breed, country of origin, disease severity, sampling type, year, and behaviour within an outbreak. No clear associations for breed, country, sampling type and year were determined in this study. ST-10 and 123 strains were present within all disease categories, from no clinical signs to severe disease. Assessment of S. zooepidemicus infection in 3 UK outbreaks at the same location found ST-10, 18, 123 strains, and a ST-173 strain in a US outbreak, were associated with haemorrhagic pneumonia and persisted in kennelled populations over time. The ST-173 clonal complex has been noted to have severe virulence capabilities in dogs and other species. S. zooepidemicus seems to thrive in environments with a high risk of transmissibility, overcrowding, stress and naïve populations, particularly for those in shelters/kennels. MLST alone cannot determine the virulence phenotype of S. zooepidemicus in dogs. However, a level of conservancy and diversity within ST allelic loci aids the opportunity to cause severe disease in dogs. Thus, further research into whole genome sequencing and characterising the virulence factors of S. zooepidemicus is warranted in dogs.

mcqs.q: Streptococcus zooepidemicus is a significant shelter/kennel pathogen in dogs. Which clinical presentation has been specifically associated with the ST-173 clonal complex in kennelled populations?
o: Urinary tract infection with bacteriuria
Hemorrhagic pneumonia
Chronic otitis externa
Subclinical bacteremia without clinical signs
mcqs.e: The ST-173 strain was associated with hemorrhagic pneumonia in a US kennel outbreak and has noted severe virulence capabilities in dogs and other species.

mcqs.q: This study of 149 S. zooepidemicus isolates from dogs found that MLST sequence types ST-10 and ST-123 were present across all disease severity categories. What is the most important clinical implication of this finding for shelter veterinarians?
o: Dogs positive for ST-10 or ST-123 are safe to house with other dogs
MLST sequence type alone cannot reliably predict virulence or disease severity in individual dogs
ST-10 and ST-123 strains are exclusively associated with sub-clinical carriage
Only whole-genome sequencing is needed for routine shelter outbreak investigations
mcqs.e: The finding that ST-10 and ST-123 were present across all disease categories (no clinical signs to severe disease) demonstrates that MLST alone cannot determine virulence phenotype, limiting its use for predicting individual disease risk.

mcqs.q: S. zooepidemicus is described as thriving in which type of environment? This is directly relevant to animal shelters.
o: Outdoor free-roaming settings with low animal density
Environments with high transmissibility, overcrowding, stress, and naive populations
Immunocompromised geriatric animals in home settings
Veterinary hospitals with high disinfection standards
mcqs.e: The paper explicitly states S. zooepidemicus 'seems to thrive in environments with a high risk of transmissibility, overcrowding, stress and naïve populations, particularly for those in shelters/kennels.'

title: Canine parvovirus is shed infrequently by cats without diarrhoea in multi-cat environments
authors: Carrai M, Decaro N, Van Brussel K, Dall'Ara P, Desario C, Fracasso M, Šlapeta J, Colombo E, Bo S, Beatty JA, Meers J, Barrs VR
abstract: Whether subclinical shedding of canine parvovirus (CPV) by cats might contribute to the epidemiology of canine CPV infections, particularly in facilities housing both cats and dogs, requires clarification. Conflicting results are reported to date. Using conventional PCR (cPCR) to amplify the VP2 gene, shedding of the CPV variants (CPV-2a, 2b, 2c) by healthy cats in multi-cat environments was reportedly common in Europe but rare in Australia. The aim of this study was to determine whether low-level faecal CPV shedding occurs in multi-cat environments in Australia and Italy using a TaqMan real-time PCR to detect Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 (CPV and feline parvovirus, FPV) DNA, and minor-groove binder probe real-time PCR assay to differentiate FPV and CPV types and to characterize CPV variants. In total, 741 non-diarrhoeic faecal samples from shelters in Australia (n = 263) and from shelters or cat colonies in Italy (n = 478) were tested. Overall, Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 DNA was detected in 49 of 741 (6.61%) samples. Differentiation was possible for 31 positive samples. FPV was most common among positive samples (28/31, 90.3%). CPV was detected in 4/31 samples (12.9%) including CPV-2a in one sample, CPV-2b in another and co-infections of FPV/CPV-2b and CPV-2a/CPV-2b in the remaining two samples. A high rate of subclinical FPV infection was detected in one shelter during an outbreak of feline panleukopenia, during which 21 of 22 asymptomatic cats (95.5%) sampled were shedding FPV. Faecal shedding of CPV by cats in multi-cat environments is uncommon suggesting that domestic cats are not significant reservoirs of CPV.

mcqs.q: In a shelter housing both cats and dogs, staff are concerned that asymptomatic cats may be shedding canine parvovirus (CPV) and infecting dogs. Based on this multi-site shelter study of 741 non-diarrhoeic fecal samples, what is the most accurate conclusion?
o: CPV shedding by asymptomatic cats is common and cats are a significant reservoir for dogs
CPV shedding by asymptomatic cats is uncommon; cats are unlikely to be significant CPV reservoirs for dogs
All cats shedding protoparvovirus were shedding CPV variants
FPV was not detected in this study population
mcqs.e: CPV was detected in only 4/31 differentiated positive samples (12.9%), while FPV predominated (90.3%). The authors conclude that 'domestic cats are not significant reservoirs of CPV,' meaning cats sharing facilities with dogs do not pose a significant CPV risk.

mcqs.q: During a feline panleukopenia outbreak at one shelter in this study, how many of the sampled asymptomatic cats were shedding FPV by real-time PCR?
o: Approximately 50% (11/22)
Approximately 25% (5-6/22)
Approximately 95% (21/22)
Approximately 10% (2/22)
mcqs.e: During the panleukopenia outbreak, 21 of 22 asymptomatic cats (95.5%) were shedding FPV, highlighting the importance of testing all cats — not just symptomatic ones — during an outbreak for isolation decisions.

mcqs.q: The overall prevalence of Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 DNA in non-diarrhoeic fecal samples from shelter cats and cat colonies was approximately:
mcqs.e: Overall, 49 of 741 (6.61%) non-diarrhoeic samples tested positive for Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 (CPV+FPV), predominantly FPV, indicating a meaningful rate of subclinical parvovirus shedding in multi-cat environments.

title: Isolation and characterization of Chlamydia felis and its pathogenesis in cats
authors: Chen J, Long J, Zhou H, Huang C, Zhu Y, Wang R, Zhang H, Qin Y, Ouyang K, Wei Z, Huang W, Chen Y
abstract: Feline upper respiratory tract disease (URTD) is a common but complicated disease that occurs in domestic cats, worldwide. 396 cats in Guangxi Province, China were screened for URTD-associated pathogens from March 2022 to August 2023. Mycoplasma felis was found to be the most prevalent infectious agent with a positivity rate of 24.75%, followed by feline calicivirus (FCV), Chlamydia felis, feline herpesvirus 1 (FHV-1) and feline influenza A virus (FeIAV) with rates of 15.91, 11.62, 5.56 and 1.52%, respectively. In particular, C. felis and M. felis were found in 13 of 55 co-infected cats. Of the 46 C. felis-positive samples, one strain, named as GXNN36, was successfully isolated using chicken embryos and it was characterized both in vivo and in vitro. For the cat studies, both high- and low-dose challenged groups showed severe conjunctivitis, accompanied by transient fever and respiratory symptoms. C. felis replicated well in turbinate, trachea and lung tissues with high copy numbers and the infection subsequently spread to the livers, spleens, pancreas, kidneys, hearts and intestines. These findings will help our understanding of the role of C. felis in feline URTD and provide a valuable model to evaluate the efficacy of vaccines and therapeutic remedies in the future.

mcqs.q: In a surveillance study of 396 cats with upper respiratory tract disease (URTD), which pathogen had the highest detection rate?
o: Feline calicivirus (FCV)
Chlamydia felis
Mycoplasma felis
Feline herpesvirus 1 (FHV-1)
mcqs.e: Mycoplasma felis had the highest positivity rate at 24.75%, followed by FCV (15.91%), C. felis (11.62%), FHV-1 (5.56%), and feline influenza A virus (1.52%).

mcqs.q: In experimental Chlamydia felis challenge of cats, the primary clinical sign was severe conjunctivitis. Where else did the organism replicate to high copy numbers beyond the upper respiratory tract?
o: Bladder and kidneys exclusively
Liver, spleen, pancreas, kidneys, heart, and intestines
Brain and spinal cord causing neurological signs
Only in conjunctival and nasal tissues without systemic spread
mcqs.e: C. felis replicated well in turbinate, trachea, and lung tissues, and subsequently spread to the livers, spleens, pancreas, kidneys, hearts, and intestines, demonstrating its potential for systemic infection beyond classic ocular signs.

mcqs.q: A shelter sees a cat with severe conjunctivitis and mild respiratory signs. Chlamydia felis co-infection with which other pathogen was found in 13 of 55 co-infected cats in this study?
o: Feline herpesvirus 1 (FHV-1)
Feline calicivirus (FCV)
Mycoplasma felis
Feline influenza A virus
mcqs.e: C. felis and Mycoplasma felis were found as co-infections in 13 of 55 co-infected cats, making M. felis the most important co-pathogen with C. felis in this URTD surveillance.

title: Feline leukemia virus in owned cats in Southeast Asia and Taiwan
authors: Capozza P, Lorusso E, Colella V, Thibault JC, Tan DY, Tronel JP, Halos L, Beugnet F, Elia G, Nguyen VL, Occhiogrosso L, Martella V, Otranto D, Decaro N
abstract: Feline leukaemia virus (FeLV) is a retrovirus associated with fatal disease in cats with infection in its progressive form. The researchers assessed FeLV circulation across Southeast Asian countries and Taiwan during 2017–2018 using ELISA and nested PCR testing. Of 47 FeLV-positive cats, 32 were confirmed positive through molecular testing. Detection rates varied significantly by location, with frequency of occurrence of FeLV proviral DNA ranging from 0% (0/43 positive samples) in Indonesia to 18.5% (22/119 positive samples) in Thailand. Statistical analysis revealed associations between FeLV positivity and country origin, age, lifestyle, and oral mucosal abnormalities. The authors conclude that additional research is necessary to better understand FeLV distribution patterns across the region.

mcqs.q: In this FeLV survey of owned cats across Southeast Asia and Taiwan, which factor was significantly associated with FeLV positivity?
o: Sex (male cats only)
Coat color
Lifestyle (outdoor access, contact with other cats)
Vaccination history for other respiratory pathogens
mcqs.e: Statistical analysis revealed associations between FeLV positivity and country of origin, age, lifestyle, and oral mucosal abnormalities. Lifestyle (including outdoor access and contact with other cats) reflects the bite-wound transmission route of FeLV.

mcqs.q: Among the Southeast Asian countries surveyed, which country had the highest FeLV proviral DNA detection rate?
o: Indonesia (0%)
Thailand (18.5%)
Vietnam (5%)
Taiwan (3%)
mcqs.e: FeLV proviral DNA frequency ranged from 0% in Indonesia to 18.5% in Thailand, demonstrating significant geographic variation in FeLV prevalence across the region.

mcqs.q: FeLV is associated with oral mucosal abnormalities. In shelter intake screening, which clinical finding in a cat should prompt FeLV testing according to the pattern identified in this study?
o: Unilateral nasal discharge only
Oral mucosal abnormalities such as stomatitis or ulceration
Skin pruritus and alopecia
Subcutaneous mass in dorsal cervical region
mcqs.e: Oral mucosal abnormalities were significantly associated with FeLV positivity in this study. Oral ulceration and stomatitis in shelter cats should prompt FeLV testing as part of the diagnostic workup.

title: Seroprevalence and risk factors for Toxoplasma gondii exposure in Australian feral and stray cats using an in-house modified agglutination test
authors: Liyanage KLDTD, Amery-Gale J, Uboldi AD, Adriaanse K, Firestone SM, Tonkin CJ, Jabbar A, Hufschmid J
abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a globally distributed zoonotic protist, capable of infecting all warm-blooded animals. In Australia, cats (Felis catus) are the only definitive host capable of spreading T. gondii infection via oocysts. Free-roaming cats are widespread in Australia and can play a central role in the ecology of T. gondii. Therefore, understanding the epidemiology of this parasite in stray and feral cats is essential to understanding the potential risk of infection in animals and humans. Due to a lack of easily accessible commercial kits, an in-house modified agglutination test (MAT) was established to test for IgG antibodies against T. gondii, using cell culture-derived T. gondii tachyzoites, and compared with a commercial MAT. A total of 552 serum samples collected during 2018–2021 from stray (n = 456) and feral cats (n = 90) (samples with missing data n = 6) from four Australian states, representing different age groups of both sexes, were screened for antibodies against T. gondii. Risk factors for T. gondii infection were assessed using multivariable logistic regression analysis. The in-house MAT had excellent agreement with the commercial MAT and provided a reliable and economical serological tool for T. gondii screening in animals. The overall observed seroprevalence for T. gondii in cats was 40.4% (223/552). Bodyweight (as a proxy for age), geographical location, season and whether cats were feral or stray, were factors associated with T. gondii seropositivity in cats. Sex was not found to be a risk factor for T. gondii infection in feral and stray cats. This study shows that Australian stray and feral cats have a high T. gondii seroprevalence, which may translate to significant health impacts for wildlife species, livestock and the public.

mcqs.q: In a serosurvey of 552 Australian feral and stray cats, the overall Toxoplasma gondii seroprevalence was approximately:
mcqs.e: T. gondii seroprevalence was 40.4% (223/552) in Australian feral and stray cats, which is high and significant given that cats are the only definitive host capable of shedding oocysts in Australia.

mcqs.q: Which of the following was NOT identified as a significant risk factor for Toxoplasma gondii seropositivity in this study of Australian free-roaming cats?
o: Bodyweight (proxy for age)
Geographical location
Sex (male vs. female)
Whether cats were feral vs. stray
mcqs.e: Sex was explicitly stated as NOT a risk factor for T. gondii infection in feral and stray cats. Significant risk factors included bodyweight (proxy for age), geographical location, season, and feral vs. stray status.

mcqs.q: From a public health perspective, why are free-roaming cats particularly important in the ecology of Toxoplasma gondii in Australia compared to other continents?
o: Australia has no native definitive hosts; cats are the only feline definitive host present
Australian cats have higher oocyst output than cats elsewhere due to unique dietary prey
T. gondii in Australia is more virulent than elsewhere and requires cat vaccination
Free-roaming cats in Australia receive no routine veterinary care, increasing parasite burden
mcqs.e: In Australia, cats (Felis catus) are the only definitive host capable of spreading T. gondii via oocysts, making free-roaming cats the sole drivers of environmental oocyst contamination with no other felid definitive hosts present.

title: Renal alterations in cats (Felis catus) housed in shelters and affected by systemic AA-amyloidosis: Clinicopathological data, histopathology, and ultrastructural features
authors: Ferri F, Ferro S, Benali SL, Aresu L, Muscardin L, Porporato F, Rossi F, Guglielmetti C, Gallo E, Palizzotto C, Callegari C, Ricagno S, Mazza M, Coppola LM, Gerardi G, Lavatelli F, Caminito S, Mazzini G, Palladini G, Merlini G, Zini E
abstract: AA-amyloidosis is frequent in shelter cats, and chronic kidney disease is the foremost cause of death. The aims were to describe kidney laboratory and microscopic findings in shelter cats with AA-amyloidosis. Cats were included if kidney specimens were collected post-mortem and laboratory data were available within 6 months before death. Renal lesions were evaluated with optical and electron microscopy. Mass spectrometry was used to characterize amyloid. Nine domestic short-hair cats were included; 4 females and 5 males with a median age of 8 years (range = 2–13). All cats had blood analyses and urinalyses available. Serum creatinine concentrations were increased in 6 cats and symmetric dimethylarginine was increased in all of the cats. All of the cats had proteinuria. Eight of 9 cats had amyloid in the medulla, and 9 had amyloid in the cortex (glomeruli). All cats had amyloid in the interstitium. Six cats had concurrent interstitial nephritis and 1 had membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. All cats had extrarenal amyloid deposits. Amyloid was AA in each case. Mass spectrometry confirmed amyloid was AA in each case. In conclusion, renal deposition of amyloid occurs in both cortex and medulla in shelter cats and is associated with azotemia and proteinuria. Renal involvement of systemic AA-amyloidosis should be considered in shelter cats with chronic kidney disease. The cat represents a natural model of renal AA-amyloidosis.

mcqs.q: In shelter cats with systemic AA-amyloidosis, which laboratory finding was present in ALL nine cats in this study?
o: Elevated serum creatinine
Elevated symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA) and proteinuria
Hypoalbuminemia
Hyperglobulinemia only
mcqs.e: Both elevated SDMA and proteinuria were present in all nine cats. Serum creatinine was elevated in only 6/9 cats. SDMA, being a more sensitive early marker of GFR decline, was universally elevated.

mcqs.q: In this case series of shelter cats with AA-amyloidosis, amyloid was deposited in which renal locations?
o: Medulla only, with cortex spared
Cortex (glomeruli) only
Both cortex (glomeruli) and medulla, with all cats also having interstitial deposits
Renal pelvis and collecting ducts exclusively
mcqs.e: Eight of nine cats had medullary amyloid, all nine had cortical/glomerular amyloid, and all cats had interstitial amyloid deposits, demonstrating widespread renal involvement in both cortex and medulla.

mcqs.q: A shelter veterinarian sees a middle-aged domestic shorthair cat with CKD, proteinuria, and elevated SDMA. Which diagnosis should be considered given this study's findings about shelter cat populations?
o: Hyperthyroidism as the underlying cause of CKD
Systemic AA-amyloidosis as a common cause of CKD in shelter cats
FIV-associated nephropathy
Pyelonephritis from ascending Escherichia coli infection
mcqs.e: This study found AA-amyloidosis is frequent in shelter cats and that it should be considered in shelter cats with CKD, azotemia, and proteinuria. Chronic inflammation common in shelter environments may drive the acute-phase SAA protein production underlying AA-amyloidosis.

title: Serial examination of the pancreas from shelter cats euthanized for population control for the prevalence of histologic and immunohistochemical changes
authors: Wu YA, Newman SJ, Lidbury JA, Steiner JM
abstract: The clinical relevance of pancreatic histologic changes in cats is unclear. Determination of clinical relevance is complicated by the focal to multifocal nature of these lesions, variable clinical presentation of affected cats, and common comorbidities. Examining the histologic changes on serial pancreatic sections from a cohort of young adult shelter cats without externally observable clinical disease could inform what should be considered normal in cats. Pancreata were obtained from 48 cats euthanized for population control. While hypoalbuminemia was common, liver enzyme activity and gastrointestinal panel results were largely unremarkable. The pancreas was sectioned every 1 cm, routinely processed, and evaluated by a board-certified veterinary pathologist. Pancreatic histologic changes were uncommon in this cohort of cats. Hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections that showed lymphocytic infiltrates were recut for CD3 and CD20 immunohistochemistry. The distribution of CD3 and CD20 positive cells and their percentages were recorded. Of 48 cats, 13 cats (27%) had localized lymphocytic infiltrates with a median percentage of affected sections of 14% (range: 7%–92%). There were no differences in observed percentages or distribution of T- or B-cells. Scattered CD3+ T-cells were incidentally identified in intralobular parenchyma. As mild lymphocytic infiltration was uncommon in this group of cats, it may not indicate a physiological response, as the anticipated response to antigenic stimulation would be expected to occur more diffusely and more commonly. Thus, the role of these infiltrates may reflect bystander inflammation or a primary pathological process (pancreatitis) and likely varies depending on the specific disease context.

mcqs.q: In a study examining pancreata from 48 clinically healthy shelter cats, what percentage showed localized lymphocytic infiltrates on histologic examination?
mcqs.e: 13 of 48 cats (27%) had localized lymphocytic infiltrates, with a median of 14% of pancreatic sections affected. This provides a baseline prevalence of subclinical pancreatic lymphocytic changes in clinically healthy young adult cats.

mcqs.q: The authors conclude that mild focal lymphocytic infiltrates of the feline pancreas may represent bystander inflammation or primary pancreatitis. Why is this clinically significant for shelter veterinarians interpreting pancreatic histopathology reports?
o: All focal lymphocytic infiltrates should be treated with corticosteroids immediately
Focal lymphocytic infiltration is so common it always represents a normal finding requiring no action
Mild focal infiltrates are uncommon in healthy cats, so their presence likely reflects pathology rather than a normal physiological response
Only B-cell (CD20+) infiltrates are clinically significant; T-cell infiltrates can be ignored
mcqs.e: Because mild lymphocytic infiltration was uncommon in this healthy cohort (27%), the authors reason it does not represent a normal physiological response. Their presence likely reflects bystander inflammation or early pancreatitis, warranting clinical attention.

mcqs.q: What sampling method was used in this study to improve detection of focal pancreatic lesions in shelter cats?
o: Single biopsy of the pancreatic head only
Fine-needle aspirate cytology of the pancreatic body
Serial sectioning of the entire pancreas at 1 cm intervals
Ultrasound-guided biopsy of visible lesions only
mcqs.e: The pancreas was sectioned every 1 cm and all sections were evaluated, specifically designed to capture the focal to multifocal nature of feline pancreatic lesions, which can be missed by single-section or limited-sampling approaches.

title: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Infection in Cats, South Korea, 2023
authors: Kang YM, Heo GB, An SH, Lee H, Park E, Cha RM, Jang YY, Sagong M, Kim AY, Kim J, Lee EK, Kim SH, Lee K, Ku B, Lee YJ, Lee K, Lee KN
abstract: In July 2023, cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) were reported at 2 shelters for stray cats in Seoul, South Korea. The cause of infection was suspected to be improperly sterilized raw food made from domestic duck meat, which was manufactured in South Korea. All viruses isolated from cats at the shelters and from the raw food belonged to HPAI A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b. The gene constellation of all viruses was most similar to that of viruses isolated in Korea in November 2022. Of note, the viruses isolated from infected cats harbored mutations E627K or D701N in polymerase basic 2, which are indicative of adaptation to mammals. Postmortem examination revealed systemic pathologic lesions and the presence of widespread virus in different tissues. Thus, consumption of raw duck meat contaminated with HPAI virus likely caused systemic symptoms and death in cats, indicating the introduction of mammal-adapted mutations of the virus.

mcqs.q: In 2023, HPAI H5N1 outbreaks occurred at two stray cat shelters in Seoul, South Korea. What was the suspected source of infection?
o: Direct contact with infected wild birds in outdoor enclosures
Improperly sterilized raw food made from domestic duck meat
Aerosol transmission from nearby poultry farms
Contaminated water from a shared water source
mcqs.e: The cause of infection was suspected to be improperly sterilized raw food made from domestic duck meat. This underscores the risk of feeding raw poultry products to shelter cats.

mcqs.q: The H5N1 viruses isolated from infected shelter cats harbored E627K or D701N mutations in the polymerase basic protein 2 (PB2) gene. Why are these mutations clinically significant?
o: They confer resistance to oseltamivir (Tamiflu) treatment
They are indicative of mammalian adaptation, suggesting enhanced replicative fitness in mammals
They reduce virus transmission between cats in shelter settings
They indicate the virus originated from H5N2 lineage and not H5N1
mcqs.e: E627K and D701N mutations in PB2 are well-established markers of mammalian adaptation of avian influenza viruses, indicating enhanced replication at mammalian body temperatures. Their presence in shelter cat isolates raises concern about pandemic potential.

mcqs.q: Postmortem examination of HPAI H5N1-infected shelter cats revealed pathologic findings that were:
o: Limited to upper respiratory tract and nasal turbinates
Confined to pulmonary parenchyma with no systemic involvement
Systemic with widespread virus detected in multiple tissues throughout the body
Predominantly neurological with encephalitis only
mcqs.e: Postmortem examination revealed systemic pathologic lesions and presence of widespread virus in different tissues, consistent with the ability of H5N1 to cause systemic infection in cats rather than purely respiratory disease.

title: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Domestic Dairy Cattle and Cats, United States, 2024
authors: Burrough ER, Magstadt DR, Petersen B, Timmermans SJ, Gauger PC, Zhang J, Siepker C, Mainenti M, Li G, Thompson AC, Gorden PJ, Plummer PJ, Main R
abstract: We report highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) virus in dairy cattle and cats in Kansas and Texas, United States, which reflects the continued spread of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses that entered the country in late 2021. Infected cattle experienced nonspecific illness, reduced feed intake and rumination, and an abrupt drop in milk production, but fatal systemic influenza infection developed in domestic cats fed raw (unpasteurized) colostrum and milk from affected cows. Cow-to-cow transmission appears to have occurred because infections were observed in cattle on Michigan, Idaho, and Ohio farms where avian influenza virus-infected cows were transported. Although the US Food and Drug Administration has indicated the commercial milk supply remains safe, the detection of influenza virus in unpasteurized bovine milk is a concern because of potential cross-species transmission. Continued surveillance of highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses in domestic production animals is needed to prevent cross-species and mammal-to-mammal transmission.

mcqs.q: In early 2024, domestic cats in the United States developed fatal systemic HPAI H5N1 infection. What was the primary exposure route for these cats?
o: Direct contact with infected wild waterfowl
Aerosol transmission from affected dairy herds
Consumption of raw (unpasteurized) colostrum and milk from HPAI-infected cows
Ingestion of raw poultry obtained from backyard flocks
mcqs.e: Cats developed fatal systemic influenza infection after being fed raw (unpasteurized) colostrum and milk from affected cows. This highlights the risk of raw dairy products as a transmission route for H5N1 to cats.

mcqs.q: What was the most characteristic clinical sign in HPAI H5N1-infected dairy cattle in this 2024 US outbreak?
o: High fever with respiratory distress and nasal discharge
Nonspecific illness with reduced feed intake, reduced rumination, and abrupt drop in milk production
Neurological signs including seizures and ataxia
Sudden death without prodromal signs
mcqs.e: Infected cattle experienced nonspecific illness, reduced feed intake and rumination, and an abrupt drop in milk production — the clinical signs that should prompt HPAI testing in dairy herds in a One Health context.

mcqs.q: This 2024 HPAI outbreak in US dairy cattle and cats highlights a One Health biosecurity concern. For farm cat populations on dairy farms, what is the most important preventive measure?
o: Annual vaccination of all barn cats with inactivated H5N1 vaccine
Preventing cats from having access to raw milk or colostrum from potentially infected cows
Monthly serology testing of all farm cats
Housing all barn cats indoors away from the dairy barn
mcqs.e: Since cats developed fatal systemic infection after consuming raw milk and colostrum from infected cows, the critical preventive measure is preventing access to raw dairy products from potentially infected animals.

title: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus in Domestic Cat, France, 2022
authors: Briand FX, Souchaud F, Pierre I, Beven V, Hirchaud E, Hérault F, Planel R, Rigaudeau A, Bernard-Stoecklin S, Van der Werf S, Lina B, Gerbier G, Eterradossi N, Schmitz A, Niqueux E, Grasland B
abstract: We detected highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b virus in a domestic cat that lived near a duck farm infected by a closely related virus in France during December 2022. Enhanced surveillance of symptomatic domestic carnivores in contact with infected birds is recommended to prevent further spread to mammals and humans.

mcqs.q: A domestic cat living near a duck farm in France was found infected with HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. What surveillance recommendation did the authors make based on this case?
o: Euthanize all cats living within 1 km of infected poultry farms
Enhanced surveillance of symptomatic domestic carnivores in contact with infected birds
Require indoor confinement of all domestic cats during HPAI outbreak seasons
Annual serological testing of all domestic cats in Europe for avian influenza
mcqs.e: The authors specifically recommended 'enhanced surveillance of symptomatic domestic carnivores in contact with infected birds' to prevent further spread to mammals and humans, reflecting a One Health approach to HPAI spillover monitoring.

mcqs.q: The H5N1 virus found in the French domestic cat was genetically closely related to the virus on which type of nearby farm?
o: Chicken layer farm
Duck farm
Turkey broiler farm
Exotic bird breeding facility
mcqs.e: The cat virus was closely related to HPAI H5N1 from a nearby duck farm, suggesting direct or indirect exposure to infected ducks as the source of feline infection.

mcqs.q: In shelter medicine, this case report is relevant because it demonstrates that domestic cats can acquire HPAI H5N1 from a novel route. What is the implication for community cat and shelter programs near poultry farms or wildlife?
o: Community cats are immune to avian influenza and require no monitoring
Community cats near poultry operations or waterfowl habitats may be a sentinel species and source of mammal-adapted H5N1 if they develop respiratory or neurological illness
Community cats should be vaccinated with avian influenza vaccine before TNR procedures
Only cats fed raw poultry diets are at risk for HPAI infection
mcqs.e: The case demonstrates cats near infected poultry can acquire HPAI H5N1 through contact with infected birds or their environment. Community/feral cats near duck farms, poultry, or waterfowl habitats represent a potential spillover interface and sentinel species for HPAI monitoring.

title: Risk Factors for SARS-CoV-2 Infection and Illness in Cats and Dogs
authors: Bienzle D, Rousseau J, Marom D, MacNicol J, Jacobson L, Sparling S, Prystajecky N, Fraser E, Weese JS
abstract: We tested swab specimens from pets in households in Ontario, Canada, with human COVID-19 cases by quantitative PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and surveyed pet owners for risk factors associated with infection and seropositivity. We tested serum samples for spike protein IgG and IgM in household pets and also in animals from shelters and low-cost neuter clinics. Among household pets, 2% (1/49) of swab specimens from dogs and 7.7% (5/65) from cats were PCR positive, but 41% of dog serum samples and 52% of cat serum samples were positive for SARS-CoV-2 IgG or IgM. The likelihood of SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity in pet samples was higher for cats but not dogs that slept on owners' beds and for dogs and cats that contracted a new illness. Seropositivity in neuter-clinic samples was 16% (35/221); in shelter samples, 9.3% (7/75). Our findings indicate a high likelihood for pets in households of humans with COVID-19 to seroconvert and become ill.

mcqs.q: In Ontario households where a human had confirmed COVID-19, what proportion of cat swab samples tested PCR-positive for SARS-CoV-2?
mcqs.e: 7.7% (5/65) of cat swab samples were PCR positive, compared to 2% (1/49) of dog swabs. The 52% figure refers to seropositivity (past exposure), not active PCR-positive shedding.

mcqs.q: SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence was measured in both household pets and shelter/clinic animals. What was the seroprevalence in shelter animals sampled in this study?
mcqs.e: Seropositivity in shelter samples was 9.3% (7/75), compared to 16% in low-cost neuter clinic animals and 41-52% in household pets of COVID-positive owners, suggesting ongoing but lower-level human-to-animal transmission in shelter settings.

mcqs.q: Which behavioral risk factor was significantly associated with SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity specifically in cats (but not dogs) in COVID-positive households?
o: Eating from the same bowl as the owner
Sleeping on the owner's bed
Going outdoors and contact with other animals
Being groomed by the owner daily
mcqs.e: Seropositivity in pet samples was higher for cats (but not dogs) that slept on owners' beds, highlighting close sleeping proximity as a risk factor for human-to-cat SARS-CoV-2 transmission.

title: Genetically Similar High-Risk Strains of Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacterales in Humans and Companion Animals, United States
authors: Xiaoli L, James AE, Stahl AL, Okumura M, Cole SD, Dietrich JM, Leeper MM, Putney JK, Walters MS, Stanton RA
abstract: To elucidate the zoonotic potential of carbapenemase-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CP-CRE) in US companion animals (i.e., dogs and cats), we queried the National Center for Biotechnology Pathogen Detection database to identify One Health clusters containing CP-CRE isolates from companion animals and humans. The 11 One Health clusters we found included most (69% [169/246]) publicly available CP-CRE sequences from US companion animals and were from 8 internationally disseminated, high-risk sequence types from 3 bacterial species (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter cloacae). All clustered isolates had New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-family carbapenemases, and most (92%) carried the blaNDM-5 allele. The One Health clusters included several closely related subclusters with geographically linked isolates from both humans and companion animals. Those results suggest that CP-CRE is an emerging One Health issue and that direct or indirect transmission of CP-CRE is occurring between humans and companion animals in the United States.

mcqs.q: A genomic epidemiology study found 11 One Health clusters linking CP-CRE isolates from US companion animals and humans. Which carbapenemase family was carried by all clustered isolates?
o: Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)
Oxacillinase-48 (OXA-48)
New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM-family)
Verona integron-mediated metallo-β-lactamase (VIM)
mcqs.e: All clustered isolates carried New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM)-family carbapenemases, with 92% carrying the specific blaNDM-5 allele, representing the most common carbapenemase type in companion animal-associated CP-CRE in the US.

mcqs.q: The study identifies CP-CRE in companion animals as an emerging One Health issue. What proportion of publicly available US companion animal CP-CRE sequences were included in the identified One Health clusters (shared with humans)?
mcqs.e: The 11 One Health clusters included 69% (169/246) of all publicly available CP-CRE sequences from US companion animals, demonstrating that most companion animal CP-CRE in the US is genetically linked to human strains.

mcqs.q: For shelter medicine, the finding of CP-CRE shared between companion animals and humans is important because it means shelter dogs and cats could be a source of transmission to which population?
o: Only immunocompetent healthy adults with no prior antibiotic exposure
Shelter staff, adopters, volunteers, and veterinary personnel — particularly those who are immunocompromised or have had recent antibiotic exposure
Only other companion animals in the shelter but not humans
Wild animal species in adjacent habitats
mcqs.e: CP-CRE transmission between companion animals and humans represents a direct zoonotic risk for shelter staff, volunteers, adopters, and veterinary personnel, with greatest risk to immunocompromised individuals or those with recent healthcare contact.

title: Giardia duodenalis in colony stray cats from Italy
authors: Guadano Procesi I, Carnio A, Berrilli F, Montalbano Di Filippo M, Scarito A, Amoruso C, Barni M, Ruffini M, Barlozzari G, Scarpulla M, De Liberato C
abstract: Study detected and genetically characterized G. duodenalis from stray cat colonies in central Italy (2018–2019). Of 133 fecal samples, 47 samples (35.3%) were positive for G. duodenalis cysts. Molecular analysis revealed 37 were positive for zoonotic Assemblage A and 2 showed a mixed infection (A + B). Sequence analysis identified Sub-assemblage AII and AIII variants. The authors noted all positive cats resulted to be infected with zoonotic assemblages, indicating stray cats as a potential human giardiasis source.

mcqs.q: In a survey of 133 fecal samples from Italian stray cat colonies, what proportion were positive for Giardia duodenalis?
mcqs.e: 35.3% (47/133) of fecal samples from stray cat colonies were positive for G. duodenalis cysts, a significant prevalence with public health relevance given that all positive cats harbored zoonotic assemblages.

mcqs.q: All Giardia-positive stray cats in this Italian colony study were infected with which assemblage type, confirming their zoonotic potential?
o: Assemblage C and D (host-adapted canine assemblages)
Assemblage E (livestock assemblage)
Assemblage A (zoonotic)
Assemblage F (host-adapted feline assemblage)
mcqs.e: All positive cats were infected with zoonotic Assemblage A (Sub-assemblages AII and AIII) or mixed A+B infections. No host-adapted feline assemblages (F) were detected, confirming that these stray cats represent a public health risk for human giardiasis.

mcqs.q: A shelter veterinarian is asked about the public health risk of adopting out cats from a stray cat colony known to have high Giardia prevalence. Based on this study's findings, the appropriate guidance is:
o: No risk; feline Giardia assemblages are exclusively host-specific and cannot infect humans

Stray cats from colonies can carry zoonotic Giardia assemblages (A/B) and should be tested and treated before adoption, especially where adopters include immunocompromised individuals or young children
Only cats with diarrhea shed zoonotic Giardia; formed fecal output means no risk
Giardia from cats is only a risk to dogs, not to humans
mcqs.e: This study found all Giardia-positive stray colony cats harbored zoonotic Assemblage A, establishing them as a potential source of human giardiasis. Pre-adoption testing and treatment, plus handwashing guidance for adopters, is warranted.

title: New insight into genetic diversity of zoonotic-potential Ancylostoma ceylanicum in stray cats living in Bangkok, Thailand, based on deep amplicon sequencing
authors: Jitsamai W, Kamkong P, Traub RJ, Taweethavonsawat P
abstract: Study characterized hookworms from stray cats in Bangkok. Of 56 hookworm-positive fecal samples, 96.4% were identified as Ancylostoma ceylanicum and 1.8% as A. caninum. Deep amplicon sequencing of the partial COI gene revealed 19 haplotypes (AC01-AC19) with three considered zoonotic. The predominant haplotype AC01 was clustered with H01-a zoonotic haplotype. Researchers concluded that deep amplicon sequencing effectively determined genetic variation, zoonotic potential, and host-parasite relationships.

mcqs.q: In Bangkok stray cats, which hookworm species predominated (96.4% of positive samples) and is known to have zoonotic potential for cutaneous larva migrans in humans?
o: Ancylostoma caninum
Ancylostoma braziliense
Ancylostoma ceylanicum
Uncinaria stenocephala
mcqs.e: Ancylostoma ceylanicum comprised 96.4% of hookworm-positive samples. Unlike A. caninum which typically causes cutaneous larva migrans, A. ceylanicum can actually establish patent intestinal infections in humans in addition to cutaneous migration.

mcqs.q: Deep amplicon sequencing of the COI gene in A. ceylanicum from Bangkok stray cats identified 19 haplotypes. What aspect of the predominant haplotype AC01 is particularly concerning from a public health perspective?
o: It is resistant to common anthelmintics including fenbendazole
It was clustered with a known zoonotic haplotype (H01), indicating human infection potential
It exclusively infects immunocompromised individuals
It represents an entirely new species unrelated to other Ancylostoma
mcqs.e: The predominant haplotype AC01 clustered with H01, a known zoonotic haplotype, indicating that the most common hookworm in Bangkok stray cats has confirmed zoonotic potential for human infection.

mcqs.q: For TNR (trap-neuter-return) programs managing stray cat colonies in Southeast Asia, this study suggests which intervention should be considered beyond sterilization?
o: Monthly bathing to remove hookworm larvae from fur
Antiparasitic treatment for hookworms given the high prevalence of zoonotic A. ceylanicum in stray cat feces
Fencing all colony sites to prevent human contact
Mass vaccination against hookworm using experimental vaccines
mcqs.e: Given 96.4% of hookworm-positive stray cats carried zoonotic-potential A. ceylanicum, antiparasitic treatment (e.g., with fenbendazole or pyrantel) should be integrated into TNR programs to reduce human exposure risk.

title: Serological and Molecular Surveillance of Influenza A Virus in Dogs and Cats in Central Chile
authors: Baumberger C, Di Pillo F, Sanchez F, Sepúlveda A, Marambio V, Orozco K, Tapia D, Hamilton-West C, Sharp B, Schultz-Cherry S, Jiménez-Bluhm P
abstract: Study evaluated influenza A virus circulation in companion animals from Chilean shelters and households (June–November 2020). IAV was detected by RT-qPCR in 3.2% (11/342) of dogs and 5.8% (4/69) of cats. Serological analysis revealed 55.5% (96/173) of dogs and 50.0% (10/20) of cats with IAV seropositivity. The study presented the first report of IAV detection in cats in South America and emphasized incorporating pets into surveillance frameworks under One Health approaches.

mcqs.q: In Chilean shelter and household animals sampled during 2020, serological IAV seroprevalence was notably high. Approximately what proportion of dogs were seropositive for influenza A?
mcqs.e: Serological analysis revealed 55.5% (96/173) of dogs were IAV-seropositive, a much higher figure than the 3.2% active PCR detection rate, demonstrating that past exposure is far more common than active detectable infection.

mcqs.q: This Chilean surveillance study had a notable 'first' for South America regarding influenza A in companion animals. What was it?
o: First detection of H5N1 in cats in South America
First report of IAV detection in cats in South America
First isolation of pandemic H1N1 from shelter dogs
First canine influenza virus (H3N8) identified in South American dogs
mcqs.e: The study presented the first report of IAV detection (by RT-qPCR) in cats in South America, highlighting that surveillance data from this region has been lacking and pets may be understudied IAV hosts.

mcqs.q: The significant discrepancy between RT-qPCR detection rates (3–6%) and seroprevalence (50–55%) in this study reflects which important epidemiological concept?
o: Cross-reactive antibody from prior vaccination
The transient nature of active IAV infection means PCR captures only current shedders while serology reveals cumulative past exposure
False-positive serology due to high background antibody in South American dogs
IAV does not replicate productively in pets, so only passive transfer of antibodies occurs
mcqs.e: The discrepancy between low PCR positivity (3–6%) and high seropositivity (50–55%) reflects that PCR detects only active infection during the short shedding window, while serology captures past exposure. This means influenza is much more common in companion animal populations than active testing suggests.

title: Serological exposure to influenza A in cats from an area with wild birds positive for avian influenza
authors: Villanueva-Saz S, Martínez M, Rueda P, Pérez MD, Lacasta D, Marteles D, Ruíz H, Gonzalez A, Verde MT, Pardo J, Arias M, Peña-Fresneda N, Fernández A, Trotta M
abstract: A cross-sectional study of 183 stray cats in Spain from 2022–2023 measured anti-influenza A antibodies using ELISA. Four of the 183 animals tested showed anti-influenza A antibodies by ELISA, yielding a seroprevalence of influenza A of 2.19%. The researchers concluded that based on this low prevalence, cats did not have an important epidemiological role in influenza A transmission during this period.

mcqs.q: In 183 stray cats from an area of Spain with documented avian influenza in wild birds (2022–2023), the ELISA-determined anti-influenza A seroprevalence was:
o: 0% (no seropositive cats detected)
mcqs.e: Seroprevalence was 2.19% (4/183 cats). Despite living in an area with HPAI-positive wild birds, the low seroprevalence led the authors to conclude cats did not play an important epidemiological role in influenza A transmission during that period.

mcqs.q: Comparing the Spanish stray cat seroprevalence study (2.19%) to the Chilean companion animal study (~50-55%), what conclusion about IAV in free-roaming cats is best supported?
o: IAV seroprevalence in cats is uniformly low worldwide regardless of exposure risk
IAV seroprevalence in cats varies substantially by geography, season, and local influenza A activity in bird and animal populations
Stray cats consistently have higher IAV exposure than owned cats in all settings
ELISA testing is unreliable for IAV serosurveillance in cats
mcqs.e: The contrast between 2.19% in Spanish stray cats during an HPAI season versus 50% in Chilean shelter/household cats demonstrates that IAV seroprevalence in cats varies substantially by geography, local circulating strains, and exposure context — consistent with spillover being an opportunistic rather than universal event.

mcqs.q: This stray cat influenza serosurveillance study was conducted in an area with avian influenza in wild birds. What was the primary rationale for testing stray cats in this sentinel surveillance context?
o: Stray cats are known to efficiently transmit avian influenza to poultry
Cats are predators and scavengers of wild birds and thus at the interface between avian influenza reservoirs and terrestrial mammal populations
Cats were believed to be amplifying hosts that could increase avian influenza virulence
Mandatory EU regulation requires annual influenza testing of all community cat colonies
mcqs.e: Cats that hunt or scavenge wild birds are at the interface between avian influenza reservoirs and terrestrial mammals, making them a logical sentinel species for spillover monitoring when HPAI is circulating in wild birds.
